stories.headline: ‘National security first’: RSS-linked group demands Centre deny entry to Elon Musk's Starlink
stories.title: ‘National security first’: RSS-linked group demands Centre deny entry to Elon Musk's Starlink
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'national security' in title weight 70
article_sentences: The Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM), an affiliate of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), asks the Centre to block Starlink’s entry into India over national security concerns and Elon Musk’s public comments against Mukesh Ambani.

New Delhi: The Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM), an affiliate of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), on Tuesday called on the Union government to withhold permission for Elon Musk’s Starlink to launch commercial satellite broadband operations in India.
The group also strongly criticized "irresponsible" comments made by Musk targeting industrialist Mukesh Ambani and indirectly referencing the Indian government.

The developments follow Musk's intensified public criticism of Ambani on Saturday, where he shared media reports alleging that a Reliance-backed company aided social media campaigns for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and made substantial political contributions to the ruling party.

Earlier, Musk referred to Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani” on platform X, accusing him of maintaining a monopoly and blaming him for the administrative delays surrounding Starlink's satellite service rollout in the country.

While Reliance has refrained from making public comments on Musk’s allegations, the Centre maintained that India’s regulatory and authorisation system for telecommunications and satellite services remains “fair and non-discriminatory”, dismissing any claims of selective treatment as “baseless and misconceived”.
Ashwani Mahajan, SJM national co-convenor, asserted that India is fully justified in denying Starlink operating rights if the firm fails to resolve the country's national security considerations.

“The organisation is of the firm belief that blocking Starlink would send a message to trade partners like the US… that India is certainly within its rights to block Starlink based on its genuine national security concerns,” he stated.

Condemning Musk’s statements, Mahajan noted that while Starlink has applied for a commercial satellite broadband license, the application remains under review and has neither been approved nor rejected.

“It is unfortunate that instead of responding to clarifications sought from his company, on national security grounds, Elon Musk has chosen to make allegations on Indian businesses and the government indirectly,” Mahajan said.
He further suggested that Starlink might be attempting to bypass regulatory hurdles by influencing public opinion or that Musk’s reactions stem from difficulty in meeting statutory obligations.
“It appears that Starlink is perhaps not prepared to meet those specific requirements.

stories.headline: Was Pinarayi ministry earnest about rebuilding Kerala after 2018 floods? CAG says no
stories.title: Was Pinarayi ministry earnest about rebuilding Kerala after 2018 floods? CAG says no
stories.summary: A CAG report exposed severe irregularities in Kerala's post-flood road reconstruction projects, including unauthorised sub-contracting, fraudulent completion bonuses, and major contractual deviations that benefited contractors at public expense.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: After the apocalyptic destruction unleashed by the 2018 floods, the Pinarayi Vijayan government projected the Rebuild Kerala Initiative (RKI) as the embodiment of Kerala's resilience.
RKI was supposed to be the dedicated agency to coordinate and implement recovery and reconstruction efforts.
Its mandate was to adopt world-class ecology-sensitive technology to insulate Kerala against future disasters.
But how shoddily and carelessly such a fight back was mounted is revealed in the report of the Comptroller and Auditor General that was tabled in the Assembly on Tuesday.
It was as if resilience was forgotten the moment the waters receded.
Under RKI, 29 PWD roads with a total length of 718.94 km across 13 districts were selected for reconstruction, with a sanctioned cost of ₹5119.54 crore.
The CAG put the microscope on 10 of these roads.

The audit noticed deficiencies in the preparation of detailed project reports, bidding documents and several instances of deviation from contractual provisions, all of which ended up causing project delays, recurring design changes and undue benefit to contractors.
Take, for instance, how irresponsibly, and in utter violation of the contract clause, work on the Uravanchal-Maruthayi stretch in North Kerala was carried out.
Clause 3.2.1 of the Engineering Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract prohibits sub-contracting beyond 25 per cent of the contract price.
Clause 3.2.2 mandates prior intimation to the Authority if any sub-contract exceeds five per cent of the contract price.
Unauthorised sub-contracting constitutes ‘Contractor Default’ under Clause 23.1.1(i), and Clause 23.1.2 empowers the Authority to terminate the contract with 15 days' notice.

stories.headline: Delhi High Court Directs Authorities To Provide Industrialist Anil Ambani's Son Details Of LOC Against Him
stories.title: Delhi High Court Directs Authorities To Provide Industrialist Anil Ambani's Son Details Of LOC Against Him
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Delhi High Court has directed the authorities to provide Jai Anshul Anil Ambani, son of industrialist Anil Ambani, specific details of the Look Out Circular (LOC) issued against him, including the date of its issuance, and a copy of the formal order.
Justice Mini Pushkarna passed the direction while hearing an application filed by Jai Anshul seeking compliance of an earlier order passed on September 17 by a coordinate bench.

The Court was informed that the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) had communicated to Jai Anshul on October 05 that an LOC had been issued against him in view of an ongoing investigation and that it continued to remain in force.
However, his counsel submitted that the communication was vague and did not disclose specific details regarding the LOC.
Taking note of the communication, the Court directed the authorities to provide details regarding when the LOC was issued and furnish a copy of the formal order to Jai Anshul in accordance with law.
The Court also took note of Ambani's submission that the communication was received only from the SFIO and not from the Bureau of Immigration.

“Accordingly, respondents are further directed to apprise the Court as to whether any other LOC has been issued against the petitioner, which is in the knowledge of the Bureau of Immigration,” the Court said.

During the hearing, counsel for the authorities submitted that the earlier direction had required the petition to be treated as a representation and requisite intimation to be provided within a time-bound manner.
It was argued that the Court had not directed the authorities to furnish specific details of the LOC.
The respondents also submitted that if Jai Anshul was dissatisfied with the communication issued by the SFIO, he could pursue other remedies available to him.
The matter will be considered next on October 16.

stories.headline: All about Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner at the centre of the SIR row
stories.title: All about Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner at the centre of the SIR row
stories.summary: Here’s a look at who Gyanesh Kumar is, what the objections are about, and where things currently stand.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Kumar, a 1988-batch IAS officer who took charge as CEC in February 2025, has defended the process as lawful and in line with Election Commission procedures.
The Election Commission has said internal differences among commissioners are part of normal institutional deliberation.
Here’s a look at who Gyanesh Kumar is, what the objections are about, and where things currently stand.
Why Gyanesh Kumar is at the centre of SIR controversy?
In late September 2026, Indian Express reported on the differences between the three-member Election Commission, placing Gyanesh Kumar's leadership under scrutiny.
Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi reportedly objected on record around 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said were taken without their knowledge.
Their objections reportedly concerned the SIR of electoral rolls, changes to voter registration Form 6, and the handling and control of electoral roll data.
Opposition parties, including the Congress, have alleged that eligible voters are being excluded and the process favoured the ruling BJP.
Not only did the poll body deny these allegations, Kumar also challenged Rahul Gandhi to substantiate his allegations of vote theft or apologise.
After criticism over the deletion of around 13 crore voters, the ECI ordered a special enrolment drive for voters left out during the SIR process.
Born in 1964, he received his schooling in Gorakhpur, Lucknow and Kanpur.
He topped the UP Board exams in high school in 1979 and intermediate in 1981.

stories.headline: Goa Fresh to expand market reach for farm producers
stories.title: Goa Fresh to expand market reach for farm producers
stories.summary: The initiative gains significance against the backdrop of supply disruptions during the Covid-19 pandemic, which exposed Goa’s dependence on neighbouring States for daily food supplies
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Goa has launched ‘Goa Fresh’, a brand initiative aimed at giving the State’s agricultural produce a distinct identity, improving market access for farmers and reducing dependence on supplies from neighbouring States.
Launched as part of the government’s Swayampurna Goa initiative, the programme seeks to connect local growers with high-value markets, including hotels, retail outlets and e-commerce platforms.
“When we launched Swayampurna Goa, our commitment was simple: make our state self-reliant and back our own people.
Goa Fresh is the next big step in that journey.
It is not just another government scheme on paper; it is our brand of pride.

We want to give Goan farmers modern packaging, strict quality standards, and direct access to high-value markets, whether that’s our thriving hotel industry, retail stores, or e-commerce,” said Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant.
The initiative gains significance against the backdrop of supply disruptions during the Covid-19 pandemic, which exposed Goa’s dependence on neighbouring States for daily food supplies.
Over the past six years, the State has more than doubled its procurement of locally grown vegetables, according to the government.
Goan farmers who produce cashew, coconut and vegetables face challenges such as high labour costs, small landholdings and the role of intermediaries that impacts their share of consumer prices.
The government sees an opportunity to bridge the gap between local production and demand from Goa’s tourism and hospitality sectors.

With a large tourist population and a thriving hotel industry, the initiative aims to help farmers secure better prices while encouraging hotels and other institutional buyers to source more produce locally.
“Right now, our core focus is anchored in agriculture, horticulture, and floriculture.

stories.headline: SC issues notice to Centre, ECI on plea challenging blanket immunity to CEC, ECs
stories.title: SC issues notice to Centre, ECI on plea challenging blanket immunity to CEC, ECs
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice to the Centre and the Election Commission of India (ECI) on a public interest litigation challenging the blanket immunity granted to the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and other Election Commissioners under Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and the other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
reasons: source: event has 3 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: 3 independent source groups -> high confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The plea seeks revival of proceedings against current and past CEC/Election Commissioners.

The Supreme Court today issued notice on a petition filed by the Association for Democratic Reforms challenging the immunity granted to Chief Election Commissioner/Election Commissioners for actions taken in purported discharge of official duties.

A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana sought the response of the Union and the Election Commission on ADR's challenge to the constitutional validity of Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan appeared for ADR.
The petition has been filed through AoR Rani Mishra.
Briefly put, the petition seeks a declaration that Section 16 of the CEC Act is unconstitutional, void and inoperative as violative of Articles 14 and 21 and the basic structure of the Constitution.
It further seeks revival of proceedings against the present and past CEC and Election Commissioners, which came to an end as Section 16 of the CEC Act came into effect.

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no Court shall entertain or continue any civil or criminal proceedings against any person who is or was a Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner for any act, thing or word, committed, done or spoken by him when, or in the course of acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty or function."
The petition contends that Section 16 provides blanket immunity to the current and previous CEC/ECs for lifetime, which has no rational nexus with the objective of ensuring independence of CEC/ECs.
The provision places the CEC & ECs beyond the reach of any Court of law, it highlights.
"No other provision in the Constitution of India or any statute grants immunity that is at once lifelong, unconditioned by good faith, free of any sanction mechanism, and without a saving clause."
Petitioner-ADR further points out that Section 16 was not originally part of the Bill introduced.

stories.headline: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afresh
stories.title: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afresh
stories.summary: Eli Lilly has a “follow-the-sun” model for its research and development wing, which gets 20 to 25 cents of every dollar from its sales revenue. Under this model, drug development never stops, with work on new drugs ticking round the clock across centres in the United States, Europe, and India.“Lilly has become the fastest developer of drugs in the world. One of the reasons for that is a follow-the-sun model. The work actually never stops on any pipeline product. We do it round the clock. It is like a baton passing every night, constantly,” David Ricks, the global pharmaceutical giant’s chair and CEO, told Forbes India in an interview while he was in New Delhi in early October.A globally recognised breeding ground for home-grown generics giants, India is hardly known to be a hub of new drug development. So, how critical is the country’s link in Lilly’s global chain?“India’s role is hugely important,” says Ricks. “It literally does one-third of the work. Every new medicine we launch has an Indian contribution.”Additionally, the India centre has developed new systems and processes that are shared with other centres and are being adopted globally. “In this, India is really a peer to our US and European centres, particularly for clinical trials,” says Ricks.Also Read: India is an important partner for Novo Nordisk’s R&D: Martin Holst LangeFat is the fuelEli Lilly has been in India for more than three decades. Ricks says this is the company’s fourth or fifth push in the country. Earlier efforts—including a 1993 partnership with Ranbaxy, once India’s largest pharma company which eventually passed into the hands of Sun Pharma, and launches in areas such as oncology and antibiotics—failed to gain enough traction. Lilly did not have products to reach large sections of the population.It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh. It is no longer merely a large market for cheaper, generic versions of the drugs MNCs spend billions to develop, or a country where they delay introducing their new drugs for as long as possible and then bear in stoic silence the loss of revenue as generic versions rush in.India is now also a hub of drug development for them and may become one of manufacturing as well. Lilly last year committed $1 billion to expand its contract manufacturing network here. Novo, the Danish pharma giant that competes with Lilly globally, shares its rival’s sentiments.“In the obesity space also, we have always had a very strong development presence in India,” Novo’s executive vice-president of R&D and chief scientific officer, Martin Hoist Lange, said in an interview with Forbes India in late September. “So, a good proportion of our clinical trials is with people from India. Thereby also obliging ourselves to launch our products in India and making our products available for people in India. So, from an R&D perspective, India is an integral part of how we do our development.”Lilly is setting up a joint laboratory with an Indian partner, whose name it has not yet disclosed, focused on process development work. At the same time, it is working with Indian manufacturers to produce registered starting materials and other key ingredients used in some of its biggest products, including its weight loss blockbuster Mounjaro. The move is part of a broader effort to diversify supply chains.“We have all become concerned that we were over relying on one country for these,” says Ricks. Establishing an Indian base for critical inputs, he adds, has become strategically important. About a year into the effort, “it is going really well”.For now, Lilly’s manufacturing footprint in India remains export-oriented. But that could change as the demand grows. “We tend to locate our manufacturing plants near our largest markets. So far, India has not been a large market. But as India grows, we’ll need to produce more, and we can look at production close to the market here,” says Ricks.Indeed, everyone likes to have their development and manufacturing bases as close to their largest markets as possible. That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs. The other factor, the unexpected catalyst, is artificial intelligence, or AI, which is changing the mechanics of pharma research.In a blog titled, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei says: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.”Also Read: The pill that could reshape India's weight-loss marketMight of weight lossIn March 2025, Eli Lilly launched Mounjaro in India. By October, it had become the country’s top‑selling drug by value overtaking the long‑standing market leader, GSK’s Augmentin. In June 2025, Novo entered the fray with Wegovy, its obesity‑focused semaglutide injection, and launched the much-awaited Ozempic in India in December.Both Ozempic and Mounjaro make you feel full sooner and for longer. But Mounjaro, which was approved five years after Ozempic and whose chemical name is tirzepatide, acts on both GLP-1 and GIP receptors. These are specialised proteins found on the surface of cells and play an important role in how the human body processes energy. Ozempic, whose chemical name is semaglutide, works only on GLP-1.India’s weight loss drugs category is estimated to have risen to ₹2,300 crore from ₹750 crore a year prior, largely driven by semaglutide going off patent on March 20, 2026, which saw 23 Indian generic versions of it launched within 24 hours.“It is inevitable,” says Ricks. “That is a by-product of our industry.” He however adds that the flood of generics has not affected Mounjaro’s growth. Instead, he says, “It has brought more people into the market.”These would be people inclined towards weight loss drugs but daunted by their high prices. “This is part of the normal cycle of our business,” he says. The same thing happened in Brazil and Canada.How does an inventor company convince buyers to pay more for their medicines despite the presence of cheaper generics?“Starting mostly with the physicians...,” says Ricks. “Through physicians we communicate… The clinical trials we have conducted… That if they are given a choice, what is the best alternative for people with obesity, people with diabetes… Now we have cardiovascular data that shows heart protection… And point out those differences when they are recommending something to a patient. I think we have comprehensive evidence versus semaglutide that is pretty convincing to most trained doctors.”Now everything in that market needs to be assessed all over again, because the next big thing is round the corner. The market that has so far been injectables is about to receive its first dose of pills.Beyond the needleOral GLP-1 pills are expected to come to India in the first half of 2027.“It is always helpful to be the first,” says Ricks. “But in the case of cardio metabolic health, it seems less important because these are chronic medications, and often the best one rises to the top. opening: Eli Lilly has a “follow-the-sun” model for its research and development wing, which gets 20 to 25 cents of every dollar from its sales revenue.
Under this model, drug development never stops, with work on new drugs ticking round the clock across centres in the United States, Europe, and India.
body: “Lilly has become the fastest developer of drugs in the world.
One of the reasons for that is a follow-the-sun model.
The work actually never stops on any pipeline product.
We do it round the clock.
It is like a baton passing every night, constantly,” David Ricks, the global pharmaceutical giant’s chair and CEO, told Forbes India in an interview while he was in New Delhi in early October.
A globally recognised breeding ground for home-grown generics giants, India is hardly known to be a hub of new drug development.
So, how critical is the country’s link in Lilly’s global chain?
“India’s role is hugely important,” says Ricks.
“It literally does one-third of the work.
Every new medicine we launch has an Indian contribution.” Additionally, the India centre has developed new systems and processes that are shared with other centres and are being adopted globally.
“In this, India is really a peer to our US and European centres, particularly for clinical trials,” says Ricks.
Fat is the fuelEli Lilly has been in India for more than three decades.
Ricks says this is the company’s fourth or fifth push in the country.

Earlier efforts—including a 1993 partnership with Ranbaxy, once India’s largest pharma company which eventually passed into the hands of Sun Pharma, and launches in areas such as oncology and antibiotics—failed to gain enough traction.
Lilly did not have products to reach large sections of the population.
It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh.

It is no longer merely a large market for cheaper, generic versions of the drugs MNCs spend billions to develop, or a country where they delay introducing their new drugs for as long as possible and then bear in stoic silence the loss of revenue as generic versions rush in.
India is now also a hub of drug development for them and may become one of manufacturing as well.
Lilly last year committed $1 billion to expand its contract manufacturing network here.
Novo, the Danish pharma giant that competes with Lilly globally, shares its rival’s sentiments.

“In the obesity space also, we have always had a very strong development presence in India,” Novo’s executive vice-president of R&D and chief scientific officer, Martin Hoist Lange, said in an interview with Forbes India in late September.
“So, a good proportion of our clinical trials is with people from India.
Thereby also obliging ourselves to launch our products in India and making our products available for people in India.

So, from an R&D perspective, India is an integral part of how we do our development.” Lilly is setting up a joint laboratory with an Indian partner, whose name it has not yet disclosed, focused on process development work.

At the same time, it is working with Indian manufacturers to produce registered starting materials and other key ingredients used in some of its biggest products, including its weight loss blockbuster Mounjaro.
The move is part of a broader effort to diversify supply chains.
“We have all become concerned that we were over relying on one country for these,” says Ricks.
Establishing an Indian base for critical inputs, he adds, has become strategically important.
About a year into the effort, “it is going really well”.
For now, Lilly’s manufacturing footprint in India remains export-oriented.
But that could change as the demand grows.
“We tend to locate our manufacturing plants near our largest markets.
So far, India has not been a large market.
But as India grows, we’ll need to produce more, and we can look at production close to the market here,” says Ricks.
Indeed, everyone likes to have their development and manufacturing bases as close to their largest markets as possible.
That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs.
The other factor, the unexpected catalyst, is artificial intelligence, or AI, which is changing the mechanics of pharma research.
In a blog titled, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei says: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.” Might of weight loss.
In March 2025, Eli Lilly launched Mounjaro in India.
By October, it had become the country’s top‑selling drug by value overtaking the long‑standing market leader, GSK’s Augmentin.
In June 2025, Novo entered the fray with Wegovy, its obesity‑focused semaglutide injection, and launched the much-awaited Ozempic in India in December.
Both Ozempic and Mounjaro make you feel full sooner and for longer.
But Mounjaro, which was approved five years after Ozempic and whose chemical name is tirzepatide, acts on both GLP-1 and GIP receptors.
These are specialised proteins found on the surface of cells and play an important role in how the human body processes energy.
Ozempic, whose chemical name is semaglutide, works only on GLP-1.

India’s weight loss drugs category is estimated to have risen to ₹2,300 crore from ₹750 crore a year prior, largely driven by semaglutide going off patent on March 20, 2026, which saw 23 Indian generic versions of it launched within 24 hours.
“It is inevitable,” says Ricks.
“That is a by-product of our industry.” He however adds that the flood of generics has not affected Mounjaro’s growth.
Instead, he says, “It has brought more people into the market.” These would be people inclined towards weight loss drugs but daunted by their high prices.
“This is part of the normal cycle of our business,” he says.
The same thing happened in Brazil and Canada.
How does an inventor company convince buyers to pay more for their medicines despite the presence of cheaper generics?
“Starting mostly with the physicians...,” says Ricks.

“Through physicians we communicate… The clinical trials we have conducted… That if they are given a choice, what is the best alternative for people with obesity, people with diabetes… Now we have cardiovascular data that shows heart protection… And point out those differences when they are recommending something to a patient.

I think we have comprehensive evidence versus semaglutide that is pretty convincing to most trained doctors.” Now everything in that market needs to be assessed all over again, because the next big thing is round the corner.
The market that has so far been injectables is about to receive its first dose of pills.
“It is always helpful to be the first,” says Ricks.
“But in the case of cardio metabolic health, it seems less important because these are chronic medications, and often the best one rises to the top.
We saw that in the injectable market.” With the pills coming into the market, the fear is they will cannibalise injectables.
There are use cases for both.
Pills work well for patients who don’t want to inject themselves and those who prefer lower prices.
Clinical studies by Eli Lilly show that in order to maintain a certain weight over time, patients can either lower the dose of Mounjaro or switch to Foundayo, which is Lilly’s oral GLP-1.
The differentiation between Lilly and Novo’s products boils down to chemistry.
Ricks says Mounjaro (tirzepatide) has achieved massive success partly because it mimics two hormones released by the gut after a meal, helping regulate appetite and blood sugar.
Novo’s semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for obesity, works as a GLP-1 receptor.
“The basic biology works a similar way.
We have a lot of respect for our competitor,” says Ricks.
Novo’s oral semaglutide is a peptide—a short chain of amino acids—which brings its own formulation challenges: Ensuring the drug survives digestion and is absorbed into the bloodstream.
Lilly took a different approach with orforglipron (Foundayo), using a small chemical compound rather than a chain of amino acids (peptides) to activate the GLP-1 receptor.
Ricks says this approach was more challenging scientifically but made production easier to scale up.

Novo’s Lange did not reveal when his company’s weight loss pill will come to India, but emphasised that Wegovy was the only drug in the obesity space that had an established cardiovascular risk reduction, by 20 percent, and a liver risk reduction.
“And those benefits are also seen with the Wegovy pill,” he said.
He highlighted his drug’s benefits over its rival’s.
They don’t have the cardiovascular and liver benefits.
They have a small molecule GLP-1 as a tablet.
“And we are slowly but surely launching outside of the US.
So far, we have launched in three countries outside of the US, with the next being Mexico,” he said.
After weight loss.
Both Lilly and Novo are betting on differentiated therapies as they expand their India portfolios.
Beyond weight loss drugs, Lilly plans to bring medicines to India across therapies.
But for that it must grapple with standards that are not the same as the international benchmarks for registration, including local data and local clinical trials.
“Doing clinical trials in India is more complicated than other markets.
So, we are working with the government to streamline that,” says Ricks.
Dementia currently affects 8.8 million people in India, and it is expected to inflict 16.9 million by 2036.
In May 2026, Eli Lilly launched its Alzheimer’s drug Kisunla (donanemab), also known as Lormalzi in India.
It costs ₹91,688 for a 350-mg vial, which needs to be taken as an intravenous infusion once every four weeks.
This, in a price sensitive market, is expensive, made even more so by the wafer-thin health insurance coverage in the country which translates into patients paying out of their own pockets.
Lilly says all its medicines are priced as per the GDP per capita of a country.
“While Kisunla and Mounjaro may still seem expensive relative to their generic alternatives, there is a pretty big discount relative to the European or US pricing,” says Ricks.
However, it too is awake to other opportunities in India.
“From a commercial perspective, we intend to launch our products in India.
It goes beyond obesity.
In India, we are in diabetes, blood disorders, haemophilia, and sickle cell disease,” said Lange.
AI-Powered R&DAmodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away.
“That,” Ricks says, “is not the case.” Medicines live in the physical world.
Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology.
And it has to be safe.
To prove a medicine’s efficacy and safety, it needs to be tested in people who have the disease.
According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase.
Lilly is deeply invested in AI for research and development, but in a different way.
Making early-stage drug research more efficient is one.
Drawing on data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects.
These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.
In September 2025, the company launched Lilly TuneLab.
It is a collaborative artificial intelligence and machine learning drug discovery platform.
This gives smaller biotech companies free access to AI tools that can help them identify promising drug candidates.
Separately, Lilly has invested $1 billion with NVIDIA to build the largest biologic supercomputer in the world, called LillyPod.
It is training AI models to predict human biology and eventually generate ideas for new drug programmes to help supercharge drug discovery.
“It will take years to fully train models useful to scientists,” says Ricks.
Novo, in April, announced a partnership with OpenAI and in September it partnered with Anthropic.
Both the partnerships are to embed advanced artificial intelligence across its entire drug development and operational pipeline.
“AI helps to amplify the volume and the speed, but it also helps by providing more insights and analysing the data that we generate.
In the clinical space, it is also a huge productivity gain,” says Lange.
Though AI can amplify and enable research, it cannot work in isolation.
“We still need the human insights on top or in parallel with what we do with AI,” he adds.

stories.headline: Supreme Court agrees to hear Trump administration's plea over Elon Musk's DOGE records
stories.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear Trump administration's plea over Elon Musk's DOGE records
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The US Supreme Court will examine whether Elon Musk's DOGE must disclose records under federal transparency law or qualifies for an exemption as a presidential advisory body.

The battle over transparency in the Trump administration has returned to the US Supreme Court, with the country's highest court agreeing to hear a dispute over public access to records linked to Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

The court's decision on Tuesday marks the second time it has intervened in a lawsuit filed by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), a watchdog group seeking documents related to DOGE's activities during the opening days of US President Donald Trump's second term.

At the heart of the dispute is a fundamental question: should DOGE be treated as a federal agency required to disclose records under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), or can it operate outside the law's disclosure requirements as an advisory body to the president?
CREW maintains that DOGE falls within the scope of FOIA and must provide access to the records sought by the organisation.
The Trump administration, however, argues that the department is exempt because it functions as a presidential advisory body.
The legal battle has already produced conflicting rulings.
US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in CREW's favour and directed the government to expedite the processing of its records request.
An appeals court panel also backed the watchdog's position.

The administration later challenged the appeals court's decision, arguing that the panel failed to follow the Supreme Court's earlier guidance on the separation of powers and interfered with the independence and confidentiality of presidential advisers.
This is not the first time the Supreme Court has stepped into the dispute.
In June 2025, its conservative majority narrowed the scope of a lower court order requiring the government to hand over DOGE-related records to CREW.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Adjourns Delhi Protest Matter To October 15
stories.title: Supreme Court Adjourns Delhi Protest Matter To October 15
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court today adjourned to October 15 the pleas filed relating to protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Election Commission's SIR of electoral rolls.

A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was scheduled to hear the matter today, but considering Justice Mohana's ill-health, the parties expressed that they had no objection if the matters were taken up on October 15.
Senior Advocates Gopal Sankaranarayanan, Menaka Guruswamy, Arundhati Katju, CU Singh, Nitya Ramakrishnan, Indira Jaising, and Solicitor General Tushar Mehta appeared.
The Court sought the presence of a senior Delhi police officer to respond to the plea of women journalists alleging police assault during protest coverage.

On the SG's request, the Court extended the time till October 15 for filing of a compliance report pursuant to the Court's October 9 directions and the response to Shailendra Mani Tripathi's contempt petition and Dr Menaka Guruswamy's petition.

Notice was also issued today on a fresh petition filed by the Association for Democratic Reforms challenging Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioners and Other Election Commissioners Act 2023, which provides immunity to ECs for actions taken in discharge of official duties.

In a special sitting on October 11, the Court directed that there shall be no detention of any person except in accordance with the procedure established by law, particularly with respect to any assembly of peaceful and unarmed persons beyond the area where Section 163 BNSS prohibitory orders are in operation.

A bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana also directed the authorities to take down the board concerning the imposition of Section 163 of BNSS in the area around the Supreme Court, if not already done, to ensure there was no apprehension regarding access to justice, including ingress and egress to any court of law.

The Court further directed that metro and rail facilities shall function normally unless restrictions are required to be imposed keeping in mind disturbances to public order, as contemplated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution of India.

On the movement of people, the Court directed that free movement in the city be permitted subject to traffic regulations and lawyers, journalists, other professionals be not impeded in discharging their professional duties.
It further ordered that the imposition of barricades be reviewed forthwith, keeping in mind law and order and other traffic conditions.
It was also directed that internet services shall remain undisturbed in the city.

stories.headline: Punjab CM Beant Singh Assassination | Supreme Court Seeks Intelligence Bureau Inputs On Convict's Prison Transfer Plea
stories.title: Punjab CM Beant Singh Assassination | Supreme Court Seeks Intelligence Bureau Inputs On Convict's Prison Transfer Plea
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Tuesday sought inputs from the Intelligence Bureau (IB) on whether Jagtar Singh Hawara, convicted in the 1995 assassination of former Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh, can be transferred from Tihar Jail in Delhi to a prison in Punjab, after concerns raised by the Punjab government over the possible impact on law and order.

A bench of Justice MM Sundresh and Justice PB Varale was hearing Hawara's plea seeking transfer to a jail in Punjab, primarily to enable him to meet his elderly mother, who is stated to be in serious condition.
The Court said that it would consider the request after obtaining the IB's assessment of the potential security and law-and-order implications of the transfer.
The Court observed that it could not disregard the Punjab government's objections, particularly since the case involved concerns that went beyond the individual prisoner.
It said that while it was inclined to consider such requests sympathetically, it had to ensure that its order did not trigger further problems in the state.
Justice Sundresh observed that the case could not be treated as an ordinary murder case because the state had raised concerns about the continuing influence of the ideology associated with the crime.
“But how do we ignore the objection of the Punjab state?...
The larger problem is still alive.
It is not that he has got a grievance.
It's not a simple case of 302.
That A killing B, B killing C, no problem, because it goes along with the person.
But it is based upon certain ideologies, certain views.
